comparator.sourceNotes: The current 2026–2027 Mechanical Engineering/Marine Technology OER, Marine curriculum table and BEP conditions (PDF pp.30–31), was freshly retrieved and visually inspected on 8 October 2026. Its ordinary requirements control over the live webpage older category allocation and chart. Year one comprises mathematics 12 EC, mechanics 24 EC, marine theory 16 EC and Integration and Skills 1/2 totaling 8 EC: 60. Year two comprises mathematics 12, Advanced Mechanics 6, Systems and Control Engineering 6, marine theory 18, Ship Design 6 and Integration and Skills 3 at 12: 60. Year three comprises a genuine 30-EC minor, Dynamics of Marine Structures 6, Electrical Drive and Conversion 4, Ship Motions and Manoeuvring 6 and Bachelor Final Project 14: 60. All 26 individual course/project/minor components total 180 EC. Integration and Skills 1/2/3 total 20 EC; Ship Design is a separate required 6-EC project within the listed 180, not an added duplicate. Mathematics and advanced-mechanics subparts remain embedded in their parent weights. Current MT1466-26 supersedes the older MT1466 code. The formal 14-EC final project replaces the old webpage 12-EC allocation. Its current entry requirement is all first-year courses and at least 54 second-year EC. No outdated ship-production/complex-loads category is carried into the current final-year list or independently added. UCR assessment on 10 October 2026 freshly retrieved the adopted OER and visually inspected its Marine Technology table (PDF p.30). The corrected 26-component, 180-EC reconstruction and 14-EC final project remain unchanged; the older website category allocation is not reinstated.

exception.reason: The closest concept—mathematical analysis and design of vessels and marine systems—was tested before adjacent directions. UCR provides substantial calculus, linear algebra, numerical methods, probability and linear-system analysis, plus useful computational and environmental methods. It does not provide a cumulative subject sequence in mechanics, thermodynamics, hydrostatics, hydromechanics, resistance/propulsion, marine structures, ship motions or vessel design. These are the objects to which the external mathematics and control methods are applied, not merely professional accreditation requirements. General algorithms, data science and sustainability courses cannot by themselves sustain 23 non-PPD courses centred on vessels and their integrated physical systems. Related sustainable-shipping, offshore/coastal and maritime-economic directions were assessed separately; each has some genuine UCR support, but extending it into a complete curriculum would shift the organising object to general environmental science, computing or economics without enough documented maritime-system content. The conclusion concerns coherence of a complete related programme, not exact module equivalence or absence of a Marine Technology degree title.
exception.curriculumContext: The current ordinary 180-EC Marine Technology reconstruction retains 60 EC in each year, all 26 individual components, 30 EC genuine minor space and the 14-EC final project. Mathematics subparts and integration/project components are counted once. The final-project entry gate remains all first-year courses and at least 54 second-year EC. No old website category or extra thesis credit is added.
exception.ucrCourseEvidence: Reviewed all 151 enriched workbook rows, including actual descriptions and outline-derived disciplinary/method profiles, formal prerequisites and six cohort availability columns. DISGATE102, DISMATH211, DISMATH213, DISMATH214 and DISMATH314 provide calculus/linear algebra, numerical differential-equation methods and mathematical statistics that meaningfully support the four external mathematics courses. DISMATH312 directly studies engineering linear systems, transfer functions, state-space and control applications. DISGATE101, DISCOMP311/312, DISARIN211/311 and DISDATA111/211 provide useful implementation, algorithmic search, planning and empirical models; DISDATA312 studies robotics kinematics and motion planning, not hull mechanics or propulsion integration. These methods are not described as substitutes for the absent statics, strength-of-materials, dynamics, thermodynamics and hydromechanical foundations. ENSDELT111 directly studies working with natural processes for flood protection, reclamation and port development; ENSDELT211 studies delta water management and resilient infrastructure. They can inform the dredging/port context but do not teach dredger design, heavy marine transport, floating stability, offshore structural loads or subsea systems. ENSECOL311 studies marine ecosystems and human impacts, offering genuine environmental content rather than naval architecture. ENSENVI211 supplies satellite/drone GIS analysis, ENSENVI213 Earth-system modelling, and ENSENVI311 natural-water biogeochemistry and treatment; none is relabelled as ship hydrodynamics. ENSGATE101/201 establish sustainability physics, chemistry, materials and modelling; their scope does not establish mechanics, thermodynamics or structural design sequences. ENSSUST112 supplies life-cycle assessment, ENSSUST111 climate mitigation, ENSSUST311 technical/economic energy-use and renewable-solution assessment, and ENSDELT311 resource/circular-economy work. They make concrete contributions to environmental vessel performance and cleaner shipping, but not marine engine/propeller matching, electrical drives or ship-production engineering. ENSSUST211 Energy & Sustainability has no availability in any of the six cohort terms and cannot be used to rescue a schedule. ENSSUST313 is a general regionally supplied sustainability project; a ship-design or marine-propulsion assignment cannot be guaranteed or invented. BENECON111/212/311/312 can support markets, producer choices, environmental externalities and empirical economic analysis; their documented content does not supply maritime logistics, vessel exploitation, shipyard operations or ship-system design. Adding all economics or environmental courses to reach 24 would weaken the course-to-concept connection. Academic feasibility fails before accepting a 24-course set, so no invented schedule or UCR credits are encoded.

candidateAssessment.concept: Vessel design, hydromechanics, propulsion and stability
candidateAssessment.assessment: The mathematical/control and computational methods are substantive, but cannot form a complete vessel-centred programme without the cumulative mechanics, hull, propulsion, structural and design subjects to which they apply.

Port development, natural-process engineering, delta resilience and marine ecology contribute to the setting. They do not sustain offshore-platform, subsea-system, dredging-vessel and heavy-marine-transport study or their load/design progression.

candidateAssessment.concept: Maritime transport, ship production and vessel operations
candidateAssessment.assessment: Economic modelling, optimisation and computational planning offer useful methods. The workbook has no documented maritime logistics, shipyard production, vessel operations or integrated transport-system sequence; a general economics/AI programme would change the object of study.

candidateAssessment.concept: Sustainable shipping and vessel performance innovation
candidateAssessment.assessment: Marine ecology, life-cycle assessment, circular resources, renewable-energy assessment and economics provide the strongest adjacent content. They do not supply sufficient vessel-specific environmental/energy/performance study to organise a complete 23-course non-PPD programme; general Earth/soil/agricultural or business additions would not resolve that gap.
